title: Marcus Julius Crescens
description: Marcus Julius Crescens is  a plausible Roman centurion built from historical evidence gathered across the semester. After more than 15 years in the Roman army, he would have seen what war really was, not just the glory people talk about, but the cost that came with it. It was not just about swinging a sword through a man’s flesh, it was about leading soldiers through battles that were sometimes unwinnable and making decisions that determined who lived and who didn’t. Over time, glory stopped meaning much. It faded faster than the lives around him. His body would have shown this, marked by scars, worn down by years of carrying gear and fallen men, and shaped by experiences that never really leave a soldier.
author: Javen Augustus; Jamarion Augustus

title: Marcus Attilius and Lucius Raecius Felix Graffito
description: This image fits the visual evidence section because it shows a gladiator graffito from Pompeii with named fighters and fight records. It supports the point that graffiti preserved details about bouts and public memory, not just artwork. The scene is commonly identified as Marcus Attilius facing Lucius Raecius Felix.
source: Imperium Romanum. “Graffiti from Pompeii.” Imperium Romanum.
image_alt_text: Pompeii graffito showing two gladiators with names and victory marks scratched into plaster.

title: Terracotta Lamp in the Form of a Gladiator’s Helmet
description: This object works as a final visual because it shows how gladiator imagery appeared outside the arena on everyday objects. The helmet shape connects to gladiator identity and Roman visual culture.
source: Terracotta Lamp in the Form of a Gladiator’s Helmet. Roman, 1st half of 2nd century CE. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain.
image_alt_text: Terracotta oil lamp shaped like a Roman gladiator helmet with a central crest and face guard.
